item.title: Édouard Balladur, Embattled French Prime Minister, Dies at 97
item.description:
Édouard Balladur, a former French prime minister who stoutly defended his country’s contentious intervention in Rwanda’s genocide, and who fought into his 90s to be cleared of involvement in a long-running corruption scandal, died on Monday in Paris. He was 97.

To some, the conservative Mr. Balladur seemed haughty and aloof, a perfectly-tailored caricature of a French political establishment that traced its roots to elite schools such as the École Nationale d’Administration, of which he was an alumnus. Others said his polished manner underscored a preference for persuasion and diplomacy over more muscular forms of exerting his will.

Clad in bespoke suits from London’s Savile Row, he sought to project a patrician image driven by a fierce ambition for the highest office in the land. But his power reached its formal peak in his short tenure as prime minister, between 1993 and 1995. His subsequent career seemed marked by a series of setbacks and miscalculations.

Mr. Balladur failed to secure victory when he turned against his mentor, Jacques Chirac, and ran in the 1995 presidential elections. In the first round of voting, Mr. Balladur came in third and was eliminated, while Mr. Chirac prevailed in a runoff against the Socialist Lionel Jospin — and went on to ostracize Mr. Balladur and those who had supported his presidential ambitions.

Between 1998 and 2002, Mr. Balladur failed in successive bids for influential positions, including the mayoralty of Paris, and finally stepped down from Parliament in 2007 after more than 20 years as a lawmaker.

His time as prime minister coincided with two events that were to scar France’s public life and self-image. The first was the decision to send troops to Rwanda for what was depicted as a limited humanitarian intervention during that country’s bloody 1994 genocide. The second was the so-called Karachi affair, in which investigators came to suspect that kickbacks from arms deals had been used to help finance Mr. Balladur’s presidential campaign — a charge of which he denied all knowledge.

Mr. Balladur spent his time as prime minister in what was known as a “cohabitation” under President François Mitterrand, a Socialist. In Rwanda, Mr. Mitterrand was widely viewed as a close ally and friend of President Juvénal Habyarimana, a member of the ruling Hutu ethnic majority, who died in April 1994 — along with his counterpart from Burundi, Cyprien Ntaryamira — when the private plane carrying them crashed near Kigali, Rwanda’s capital.

Their deaths ignited waves of brutal killings of members of the Tutsi, a minority ethnic group, and moderate Hutus. At the time, a group of Tutsi exiles had formed a guerrilla army challenging the Hutu government from neighboring Uganda.

Reflecting its longstanding role in French-speaking Africa, France had already sent troops to Rwanda in 1990 to support the Hutu-led government against the Tutsi insurgents. When news of Rwanda’s genocide began to circulate in June 1994, France won United Nations backing for what was described as a limited humanitarian intervention by some 2,500 troops to set up a “safe haven” in the southwest of the country as an impartial force to shield civilians.

The move drew enduring broadsides from critics who accused France of bias toward the Hutu, some of whose commanders had been trained at prestigious French military schools. Paul Kagame, who emerged as the most powerful leader of the Tutsi insurgents and who later became Rwanda’s president, accused the French forces of participation in massacres within the so-called safe haven.

Mr. Balladur called Mr. Kagame’s accusation a “self-interested lie.” As late as 2021, he said in an interview with the magazine Paris Match that “our army was not a police force, its actions were humanitarian.”

“The duty to tell the truth does not lie with France alone,” he added. “Who among the world powers did more than France to stop the genocide? No one. Who even did as much as France to stop the genocide? No one in that regard, either.”

Édouard Balladur was born on May 2, 1929, in Izmir, then known as Smyrna, on Turkey’s Aegean coastline, to Pierre Balladur, a bank director descended from a family with claims to dual Ottoman and French nationality, and Emilie Balladur.

In the mid-1930s, the family emigrated to France. In 1957, the year of his graduation from the École Nationale d’Administration, Mr. Balladur married Marie-Josèphe Delacour, and they had four sons: Pierre, Jérôme, Henri and Romain.

His wife died in December. Information about his survivors was not immediately available.

Mr. Balladur held a variety of administrative positions, beginning as an adviser to Georges Pompidou, who served as prime minister and, later, as president of France from 1969 until his death in 1974. Mr. Balladur also held executive positions at the former state broadcaster ORTF and at the French arm of a company that built and operated the Mont Blanc Tunnel linking France and Italy under the Alps.

He was closely associated for many years with Mr. Chirac, who, as prime minister, appointed Mr. Balladur as the minister of economy and finance. In that role, Mr. Balladur privatized several state-owned firms, including Paribas, a financial holding company that owned an investment bank in addition to other assets. “We are working for economic democracy,” he said at the time.

When a coalition of conservatives secured an overwhelming victory in parliamentary elections in 1993, Mr. Chirac promoted Mr. Balladur as prime minister with the understanding that his protégé would not contest the presidency in elections scheduled for two years later. But Mr. Balladur went back on his word, infuriating Mr. Chirac.

During Mr. Balladur’s brief spell at the Hôtel de Matignon, the official residence of French prime ministers, commission fees and “sweeteners” were paid to middlemen and military officials on the sale to Pakistan of three French submarines.

A year after Mr. Chirac secured the presidency in 1995, he canceled those payments. In an attack that is widely thought to have been launched as revenge for the cancellation, a suicide bomber in 2002 killed 11 French technicians — who had been sent to Pakistan for work related to the submarine deal — in the southern port of Karachi.

The attack galvanized suspicions that part of the commissions — totaling around $2 million in today’s currency — had been clandestinely redirected back to France and ended up in Mr. Balladur’s campaign coffers. In 2017, when he was charged with complicity in the misuse of funds, he denied wrongdoing, as did his former defense minister, François Léotard.

In 2020, three former government officials and three others, including two Lebanese middlemen, were found guilty of misusing funds. In March 2021, Mr. Balladur, then 91, was acquitted, but Mr. Leotard was found guilty. (He died in 2023.)

During his trial, Mr. Balladur drew some mockery in France by saying that he believed that a large injection of funds into his campaign had come from the sale of T-shirts and other merchandise. But he also defended himself by referring to efforts he made during his prime ministry to tighten the rules concerning campaign contributions.

“I would be a person of singular perversity if I had, at the same time I claimed to be cleaning up public life, been trying to pollute it,” he said.

item.title: Trump Returns to a Familiar Playbook as the War With Iran Flares Up Again
item.description:
As the on-again, off-again war in Iran flares up again, President Trump seems bogged down in a conflict that he cannot control or move past, despite his declarations of total victory.

On Tuesday night, after the latest exchange of fire over control of the Strait of Hormuz, Mr. Trump called on the Iranian people to rise up — something he did at the outset of the war six months ago, before he acknowledged that his command was easier said than done.

In a social media post, Mr. Trump also brushed off the stalled negotiations with Iran.

“I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement,” he wrote on Tuesday night, hours after the United States carried out a fresh wave of attacks and Iran hit back.

“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Mr. Trump continued. “They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

The post followed a 24-hour stretch during which Mr. Trump’s by-now familiar playbook for the conflict was on full display. The president went from boasting that Iran was defeated militarily, a “failed nation” in economic disarray, to threatening an apocalyptic attack that would leave “very little left” of the country after it had defied his declarations and demands.

By Wednesday morning, as Iran and the United States assessed the damage of the most recent attacks, Mr. Trump was back to trolling the country on social media, asking his followers whether the United States should name the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait.”

Foreign policy experts say the latest round of hostilities point to a reality that has become increasingly clear of Mr. Trump’s handling of the war: He has run out of options.

“The strategy has been rinse and repeat, whether it’s rhetorical or kinetic action,” said Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist and former State Department appointee in the first Trump administration. “It’s been absolutely shocking how the United States has been exposed for a lack of a plan of engagement, and a lack of a plan to either win or exit this war.”

Mr. Bartlett said that Mr. Trump’s return to a call to action urging Iranians to take over the government — an unfulfilled objective of the war that Mr. Trump has admitted was not achievable — suggests he has no real strategy.

“When you get to the bottom,” he added, “you go back to the top of the ladder of engagement.”

But regardless of Mr. Trump’s combative words, Iran is making clear that it has leverage, as well. Even though Mr. Trump had predicted that the war would be over in a matter of weeks, there is no real end in sight. Iran has fired on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, severely curbing the ability of U.S. allies to export oil and gas.

That is not to say that the U.S. operations in Iran have not hurt the country. Michael Froman, the president of the Council on Foreign Relations, said that it was undeniable that Iran was in a fundamentally weaker position than it was a few years ago, and that the U.S. military had achieved many of the war’s objectives.

In the first weeks of the operation, the United States took out senior leaders, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and decimated Iran’s navy. Mr. Trump has also claimed that the country has “no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country.”

But Iran, now led by a more hard-line regime, has proved that it can disrupt the global economy even with a weakened or limited military, by wielding its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz.

“The U.S. has demonstrated its capacity, and that it continues to have one of the most effective militaries in the world,” Mr. Froman said. “I think the challenge is this asymmetric warfare — where we do have the most effective military in the world, but smaller powers with far less capacity, strategically deployed, could still wreak havoc and make it difficult for us to achieve 100 percent of our objectives.”

Mr. Trump has recently sought to move on from a military campaign in Iran by waging economic warfare.

The United States has sought to squeeze Iran economically by enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports and increasing sanctions on Tehran. The administration is also banking on a so-called “economic D-Day” announced last month by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, which the White House described “an unprecedented campaign to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

The campaign is intended to exert pressure on other countries, including potentially China and Russia, that continue to trade with Iran or help it evade U.S. sanctions.

But few countries have shown any indication that it plans to heed the calls, including the two U.S. adversaries Mr. Trump has been reluctant to confront.

China remains a lifeline for Iran, buying its oil and supplying it with raw materials and technology that support its economy and military. And just this week, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia pledged that his country would continue to support Iran and help them defend their national interests.

Mr. Trump is also feeling the political price at home, in terms of the toll on the American economy ahead of the midterm elections. He is reluctant to resume an all-out bombardment, even though he issues regular threats, including one on Tuesday night announcing that the United States was hitting Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack,” he wrote, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!”

Khaled Elgindy, a senior research fellow in the Middle East program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft and adjunct instructor at Georgetown University’s Center for Contemporary Arab Studies, said that Mr. Trump’s bluster on social media is attempting to save face for the quagmire he has put himself, and Republicans heading into the midterms, in.

“Part of the play is that he’s just playing to his base, whether it’s true or not,” Mr. Elgindy said. “I don’t think there’s much of a strategy beyond trying to wish things into existence by sheer force of words.”

item.title: Inside Trump’s Second Term
item.description:
If you want to understand the moment we’re in, you have to understand Donald Trump. That’s easier said than done; Trump thrives on drama — ideally in ALL CAPS on Truth Social — and prides himself on being unpredictable (although some would argue it’s all part of a strategy).

The flood of missives and missiles, of hyperbolic threats (“a whole civilization will die tonight”) and morphing deadlines coming out of the White House can seem surreal. But two of my colleagues have written a book full of riveting, granular detail that makes it feel, well, very real.

In “Regime Change,” Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan take you into the room for the key moments of the president’s second term. I spoke to Jonathan about some of them.

Jonathan, let’s start with Iran. A lot of people were baffled by Trump’s decision to go to war. What swayed him? Was it Iran’s plots to kill him? His success in Venezuela? Israel’s war pitch?

It was all those things. But also, Trump has always been hawkish about Iran.

In Term 1, he pulls out of the Iran nuclear deal. He orders the assassination of this very senior Iranian general, Qassim Suleimani. Then, when he’s out of office, he learns that the Iranian regime is trying to get hit men to kill him. Iran hacks the emails of his campaign manager. So, for Trump, this is also personal.

How important was that meeting in February you guys describe in such incredible detail, when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu persuaded Trump to actually go to war?

It was very important. I’m not aware of any historical parallel for a foreign leader going down to the White House Situation Room and pitching the American president on going to war.

That war hasn’t gone to plan. How has that affected the Trump-Netanyahu relationship?

It was always a very up-and-down, fraught relationship. Trump views Netanyahu as a strong leader but also as someone who needs to be restrained. A couple of months ago Trump started to view Netanyahu as a problem — an obstacle to getting out of this war.

He became very agitated about what Netanyahu was doing in Lebanon. And so the U.S. cut the Israelis out of their negotiations with Iran. Right now, it’s not a good relationship at all.

You write that Netanyahu, President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin were all better prepared to deal with Trump during his second term than his first. How so?

Yes, and on that list, Xi Jinping might have been the best prepared.

In April last year, when Trump essentially declares a trade war with the whole world, Xi Jinping doesn’t negotiate. He just raises tariffs himself and implements a whole bunch of restrictions on rare earths and magnets and things that the Americans need. He had this all lined up — he was fully prepared to wage economic supply chain war against the United States. And he won that skirmish.

Trump sends his Treasury secretary to Geneva to negotiate an off-ramp with China. Which he does; the tariff rates go down. And ever since then, Trump has taken a very dovish posture with Beijing.

Are there lessons for the rest of the world in this approach to dealing with Trump?

There’s this whole conversation in the international diplomatic community: How do you deal with Trump? I’ve always thought that conversation is sort of absurd. The Europeans talk about this playbook — you flatter him, bring him gifts and what have you. That might get you something, for a day or two. But what Xi Jinping showed is the way to deal with Trump is through strength.

Trump really understands leverage. He likes picking off countries one at a time so he can use the leverage of the U.S. military and economy and technology to squeeze that other party. And China — unlike some of the struggling small and middle powers — had leverage to force Trump down, in a very effective way.

What does that mean for Trump’s commitment, say, to defend Taiwan?

We have a scene in our book where he’s talking about Taiwan and he holds up a little teaspoon, basically, as a means of saying, Why would we fight over this little speck of land?

He hasn’t formally changed U.S. policy on Taiwan, but I’m not aware of anyone around him who thinks that Donald Trump would use the American military to fight for Taiwan’s independence.

Does that suggest NATO is dead, too? If the Russians march into Estonia, would the U.S. intervene?

At this point, you would have to be smoking something to think that Article 5, the mutual defense clause that is the bedrock of the alliance, is ironclad when it comes to Donald Trump. I wouldn’t want to predict one way or the other, but the notion that you could rely on him to defend a small nation against Russia is obviously questionable at best.

All this considered, how ideological is Trump, really?

Trump has never viewed the world the way American presidents of the last 50 years have viewed it, in terms of a post-World War II order and an alliance of liberal democracies. He basically sees the world as a bunch of countries that owe America money.

At a sort of cellular level, he’s attracted to strongmen and has contempt for Europeans and multilateral institutions defending human rights and international law. But that doesn’t come from a deeply held consistent worldview. If there’s an ideology, it’s “Might makes right.”

This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.

The deadly landslide and flash floods in Nepal last week were most likely caused by weakened bedrock in the glacier. My colleagues used a combination of satellite imagery and 3-D terrain models to visualize what happened.

Still standing: It’s become known as the “miracle” house. The home of the Pyakurel family survived as its surroundings were swept away by floodwaters.

U.S. strikes on Iran killed five people who were celebrating a wedding, according to Iranian officials. The U.S. military said it had not targeted civilians.

The world has failed in its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial times, the U.N. said. The organization set a new target.

Xi Jinping made his first visit to Egypt in a decade, challenging U.S. influence in the Middle East.

Joshua Wong, the prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist, pleaded guilty to colluding with Western lawmakers. He faces life in prison.

The U.S. oil giant Chevron will invest $7 billion to more than double its production in Venezuela.

Our Pentagon reporter John Ismay explains how the U.S. Navy is facing a logistical nightmare in the Middle East to support operations against Iran. Watch the video.

King Charles III will view the Bayeux Tapestry in London, 40 years after he saw it in France with Diana.

Ariana Grande wrapped up her world tour and prepared to step back from public life.

A baby boom among kakapos, a critically endangered parrot species, has resulted in a record number of chicks this year.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about the luxury Gleneagles hotel in Scotland.

A short subway ride from the U.S. Open, excitement is building in New York City’s Little Manila over Alex Eala, the breakout tennis star who has reached icon status among the Filipino diaspora. For her first-round match, supporters wore floppy hats that featured the Filipino flag and T-shirts with images of a popular Eala internet meme. “This is not Rihanna,” one post on social media said. “It’s Alex Eala.”

Aryna Sabalenka and Carlos Alcaraz headline Day 4 of the U.S. Open. Follow our live updates.

For thousands of years, we have shaped our canine companions through selective breeding. Now, dog engineering is entering a new era.

A U.S. biotech start-up said it had used the technique known as CRISPR to create gene-edited, hypoallergenic dogs. Thanks to a single genetic tweak, the pups, two adorable beagles, appear unable to produce a protein that can leave some people wheezing. It will take more research before such dogs can make their way into homes from the lab, but the development is already raising ethical questions. Read more about the concerns.

Active shooter drills are common practice in U.S. schools and universities. Now the drills are in the spotlight in Thailand and the Philippines, where recent outbreaks of gun violence have sent officials searching for solutions — searches that have veered in different directions.

The drills are not new to Thailand, which has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in Asia and where a 14-year-old boy fatally shot six people at a school last month. But they are now being rolled out in primary schools. In the Philippines, the drills were piloted by some school administrators and then paused. Some say they may do more harm than good. item.title: Joshua Wong, Jailed Hong Kong Activist, Pleads Guilty to Foreign Collusion
item.description:
Joshua Wong, a prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to collusion for lobbying Western lawmakers, a case that shows how China treats international outreach as a national security crime.

The maximum penalty for colluding with foreign forces is life in prison.

Mr. Wong was accused of conspiring with other campaigners to lobby lawmakers, particularly those in the United States like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio, to impose sanctions on Hong Kong and China. The campaigners sought to pressure officials in Beijing and Hong Kong for greater democratic rights in the semiautonomous territory.

Mr. Wong, who turns 30 next month, was one of the youngest activists in a democracy movement that was quashed in 2020 after Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law that effectively outlawed political dissent in Hong Kong.

In a sign of the sensitivity around the case, police officers in tactical vests and police vehicles surrounded the courthouse where Mr. Wong’s case was being heard on Wednesday.

He is already serving an almost five-year prison term for his role in an unofficial primary election in 2020 organized by the city’s pro-democracy camp that the authorities deemed subversive. That case, the city’s largest national security trial, led to the conviction of Mr. Wong and more than 40 other former politicians and activists.

Mr. Wong was arrested on the foreign collusion charge in June last year while in prison. On Wednesday, his lawyers urged the judge, William Tam, to consider a lighter sentence, saying Mr. Wong had matured substantially and hoped to one day leave prison so that he could take care of his aging parents.

Mr. Wong’s repeated prosecutions reflect the drastic political changes that have taken place in Hong Kong, a former British colony, since it was returned to China in 1997. At the time, Beijing agreed to preserve Western-style civil liberties that are not available in mainland China, such as freedom of speech, for 50 years.

Today, the city’s legislature is devoid of any significant opposition and independent media and members of civil society have largely been muzzled. Bookstores accused of carrying subversive books have been closed.

Mr. Wong’s plea on Wednesday came seven months after a court sentenced Jimmy Lai, a pro-democracy media tycoon, to 20 years in prison on charges of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces and conspiracy to publish seditious materials under the national security law.

The judge said that Mr. Wong would be sentenced at a later date, but did not provide any further details.

Mr. Wong rose to prominence in 2012, when at he age of 14 he led a student movement to oppose the introduction of a Chinese national education curriculum in Hong Kong. He later became one of the most internationally-recognized faces of the 2014 Umbrella Movement protests that called for people in Hong Kong to be given the right to vote for their leader. He appeared on the covers of Western magazines and was the subject of a June Pictures documentary, “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower,” distributed by Netflix.

Western legal experts say that Mr. Wong and other pro-democracy activists have not been given fair trials by Hong Kong’s judges, who are handpicked by the city’s chief executive to handle national security cases.

“It’s clear that the Hong Kong government has made a decision to keep Joshua behind bars more or less indefinitely,” said Thomas E. Kellogg, the executive director of the Georgetown Center for Asian Law. “They’re doing this precisely because he is a prominent political figure, someone whom Hong Kongers around the world respect and admire.”

“The Hong Kong government may hope that Hong Kongers will forget about him if they put him away for another decade or more,” he continued. “But I don’t think that will happen.”

item.title: Inside the Fight Against a Flesh-Eating Fly in Mexico
item.description:
The New World screwworm is a flesh-eating fly that preys on livestock and other animals. Now imagine an entire plant producing millions of such insects a week. The larvae feasts on a mixture of cellulose, egg, milk and cow’s blood that mimics flesh.

The result is a pungent, sickly sweet odor of rotting tissue — one that invades your nostrils and lingers.

“You get used to it,” said Dr. José Luis Quintero, who helps run such a laboratory in Mexico. “It’s part of the job.”

Mexican officials have been racing to combat the first major screwworm infestation in the country in decades, one that has already disrupted a strained cattle industry in both Mexico and the United States. Screwworms were largely eradicated in the region by the early 2000s, but a combination of factors has allowed the flies to make an unwelcome comeback, shutting the U.S. border to Mexican cattle imports last year and contributing to high U.S. beef prices.

In the town of Metapa, which sits along the Mexican border with Guatemala, a newly refurbished plant has become Mexico’s main solution to the parasite that has already resulted in more than 34,000 cumulative cases in all but two of Mexico’s 32 states since the first incidence was detected in November 2024. The outbreak is estimated to cost billions of dollars combined in losses and the measures to fight it.

The site, inaugurated in late June, is the only such plant in Mexico that produces sterile flies, a process that involves breeding enormous quantities of flies, sterilizing them by exposing them to radiation and then releasing them into the wild. Wild female flies then mate with the sterile male insects and slowly reduce the population size.

The goal is to produce 100 million sterile flies a week by November so that the insects can be distributed, starting with Texas and northern Mexico on down, and contain the outbreak.

The livelihoods of many depend on this multinational effort to eradicate a fly that can wreak extreme havoc.

Adult females lay their eggs, roughly 200 per batch, in the open wounds or orifices of warm-blooded animals. When the eggs hatch, the larvae burrow into the wound, consuming the animal’s tissue, thus the name screwworm. Untreated infections can kill animals within a week.

“It really is a concerning issue,” said Hunberto Gomes Velasques, who oversees the sterile fly plant in Metapa and admitted feeling the time crunch.

Late last month, the United States began a phased reopening of the border to cattle imports, though officials said the screwworm problem will persist for a while.

President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico, who originally opposed the border closing and attended the Metapa plant’s inauguration, said officials cannot say for sure how long the eradication will take but noted that the plant will help contain the spread.

“It was eradicated once before and that is why experts say we can eradicate it a second time,” she said.

Experts have estimated that eradication could take up to 20 years. When asked, Dr. Quintero pointed to history: The fly was a serious livestock scourge in the region in the early 20th century. But the United States was declared free of wild screwworms in 1966 and battled a vicious outbreak the following decade. By 1991, Mexico was also free. Ever since, with help from a U.S.-funded sterile fly production plant that opened in Panama in 2006, efforts pushed the flies back down to the Darién Gap.

It was in 2023 that cases surged in Panama and Costa Rica, and then began spreading steadily north through Mexico and eventually the United States. The Darién Gap, a narrow, jungle land bridge that connects Panama and Colombia, was the biological barrier that normally kept the screwworm at bay.

Experts said there could be several reasons the screwworm returned. Pablo Liedo, a researcher and entomology expert at the College of the Southern Border, suggested that there could have been hiccups with or a lack of attention by the authorities on the sterile insect programs.

But he also said that the hundreds of thousands of migrants who crossed the Darién Gap and headed for the U.S. border under the Biden administration might have also contributed to the latest outbreak.

“It was a very closed jungle,” Mr. Liedo said.

Flies may have hitched a ride on animals transported by humans, he said. He also pointed to illegal animal trafficking throughout the region that evades inspection, which U.S. officials have repeatedly complained about.

To tackle the new screwworm scourge, the Mexican authorities decided that the fastest way to get a sterile fly production site up and running — in a year — was to retrofit a plant in Metapa that was built in the 1970s to breed and sterilize the Mediterranean fruit fly. The Mexican government contributed $30 million to the upgrade, while the United States pitched in $21 million.

Mr. Gomes Velasques said the plant includes a sealed ventilation system so flies cannot escape and a sterilization process for any waste. There is new equipment to produce the worms’ food in-house. There are rooms heated up to 101 degrees Fahrenheit and with 80 percent relative humidity for the larvae to incubate. The plant will run 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, he said.

In July, the site was still ramping up initial production, so many sparkling new rooms sat empty. But in one, trays of pupae — a stage in the flies’ life — awaited while a constant buzz came from six nearby cages that held nearly 300,000 flies.

Mr. Gomes Velasques said then that the plant was producing about 10 million sterile flies per week. They are taken to northern Mexico, where they are dispersed by plane.

Combined with the Panama site, experts said, this wasn’t enough to fight the current regional outbreak. They estimated that at least 500 million sterile flies per week were needed. The U.S. Department of Agriculture said a new plant in Texas would open in early 2027 but would not reach full capacity, 300 million sterile flies per week, until the end of 2028.

Eduardo Farfán, the vice president of a state association of veterinarians and a veterinarian in Pijijiapan, a small Mexican town three hours from the Guatemala border, said the Mexican government was “trying to block out the sun with a finger.” The response has not been ample or fast enough, he said.

“Can it be eradicated? Yes. But it’s a question of having more,” he said. “The worm ate our time.”

Until then, frontline veterinarians like Mr. Farfán and ranchers like Francisco Javier Rodríguez have to battle the screwworm daily. Chiapas is the Mexican state most affected by screwworm, while northern Mexico along the U.S. border has had relatively fewer cases.

On a recent afternoon, Mr. Farfán accompanied Mr. Rodríguez, 38, to his plot of land to see a 3-day-old calf named Coneja that had already been infected.

The flies are difficult to combat because they are numerous, mobile and small. They can detect even tiny amounts of blood, such as a scratch on a dog’s ear or a tick bite on a horse. For ranchers, it is necessary but tedious work inspecting all their animals. (They can also use deworming medication preventively.)

Even though Mr. Rodríguez said he had applied a disinfecting solution after the calf’s birth, the site where its umbilical cord had been attached hadn’t scarred over yet, and screwworms had already burrowed in.

Mr. Rodríguez grabbed Coneja, held her down on the back of a truck as Mr. Farfán applied a blue antibacterial powder to the spot. He used tweezers to pull out 20 worms.

“There’s probably way more,” Mr. Farfán said.

Of his 50 animals, Mr. Rodríguez said, nine have been infected by screwworms over the past year, the majority of them calves. While none have died, he said, some of the cattle needed weeks to recover because the infection affected their appetites and milk production.

“I have to check every day,” he said.

Emiliano Rodríguez Mega contributed reporting.

item.title: In Small Iranian Town, a U.S. Attack Turns a Wedding Into a Tragedy
item.description:
It began like any traditional wedding in southern Iran. The women arrived with their hands elaborately decorated with henna. Children played in the courtyard. A festive meal was about to be served in a room draped with carpets and pillows.

It ended when a bomb brought down the roof, turning a night of celebration into a jumble of dust-coated sandals, torn garlands and blood-soaked rugs.

Dozens of guests, according to a witness and accounts in local news media, had already arrived at the Malahi family’s home and surrounding buildings in the southern city of Kuhestak to celebrate a young bride and groom.

Around 9:30 p.m. on Tuesday, the wedding was struck by a bomb that, according to a weapons expert and a visual analysis by The New York Times, had been released by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran. At least five wedding guests were killed, including a 6-year-old boy, and at least 67 other people were wounded, according to Iran’s Red Crescent Society, a humanitarian aid group.

Among the guests was a woman named Motahareh, whose identity was verified by The Times. The night of the wedding, she posted a selfie on Instagram from the women’s henna party the night before — beaming in perfectly applied makeup, a lilac head scarf and flowery robe.

“Last night was the first night!” she wrote. “For the coming nights, should I make these sorts of stories for you or what!!!”

In her next post, uploaded within an hour after the attack, Motahareh is in the same lilac scarf — but now, her eyes are smeared with black makeup, her face covered in red blotches.

“Tonight was supposed to be a night of love and laughter,” Motahareh wrote. “But the wedding turned into mourning, and a sweet night will forever be bitter.” She did not share her last name on her account, which was corroborated, and has not replied to requests by The Times for an interview.

A video of the immediate aftermath of the strike showed the chaotic scene of neighborhood residents with flashlights rushing between damaged buildings as emergency medical workers worked to douse the area with a hose. The Times confirmed precisely where the video had been filmed, which showed features matching satellite imagery of the area and that the video was from Tuesday evening.

Kuhestak, a port city, is close to the strategic Strait of Hormuz. The attack came as U.S. forces said they were retaliating against Iranian attacks on ships and American forces in the region. U.S. Central Command said it had struck communication sites, along with other locations it said were operated by Iran’s armed forces, which include the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

The attacks on Kuhestak hit a large communications tower near the town’s port. After the tower was struck, it crashed across a street toward a corner store and residential buildings, photos and a video verified by The Times showed.

Another attack hit a building in the residential area where the wedding was being held, around 150 yards from the communications tower, according to the accounts of multiple residents, local officials and videos that were posted by witnesses and verified by The Times.

The Times collected videos of weapons remnants filmed after the attacks on Kuhestak and shared them with Trevor Ball, a former U.S. Army explosive ordnance disposal technician and an analyst at Armament Research Services. He identified the remnants as components of a glide bomb, which is used by U.S. Central Command and not used by Iran’s forces.

Asked about the attack on the wedding and the munitions, a Central Command spokesman, Capt. Tim Hawkins of the U.S. Navy, said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.”

Iranian officials have called the attack a war crime, and Iran’s Red Crescent Society said its head had asked the prosecutor at the International Criminal Court to investigate the episode.

In the small towns of southern Iran, weddings are traditionally held in people’s homes, as was the case with the Malahi family. Weddings become a neighborhood event, with men and women gathering in separate houses. The attacks appear to have hit one of the buildings where the wedding was held.

Hamid Kasiri, a teacher, and other witnesses posted videos of the gaping hole in the roof of one building, which Iranian officials said had been directly hit by a U.S. strike. Concrete walls were punctured, doors were shattered, ceilings collapsed and debris was strewed across the area.

Mr. Ball analyzed weapons remains shown in pictures and videos taken at the scene of the strike by Mr. Kasiri, the local teacher, and a reporter for Iran’s state broadcaster, IRIB. Mr. Ball identified the remains as parts of a U.S. glide bomb. A tail fin and distinctive casing were consistent with the Joint Standoff Weapon, or JSOW, he said.

The fin recovered, in the first image below, matches JSOW fins recovered after strikes in Yemen and Venezuela, the latter in the second photo, as seen on the Open Source Munitions Portal, a database of weapon fragments found in conflict zones.

The dimensions of the recovered weapon casing and its distinctive pattern of bolt holes also match those in a reference photo of a JSOW on the weapons database.

A JSOW bomb also appeared to be loaded under the wings of a U.S. fighter jet taking off in a video published by U.S. Central Command on Tuesday alongside the statement that it had conducted strikes on targets in Iran.

The attack on Kuhestak is the fourth episode reported by The Times in which strikes on structures with no military use were hit and civilians were killed. On Feb. 28, the first day of the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, a U.S. Tomahawk missile hit an elementary school in Minab, Iran, killing civilians, most of them children, Iranian officials said.

Hours later, the United States used several PrSM missiles to strike near a residential area in Lamerd, Iran, killing 21, Iranian officials said. In July, the United States used a 2,000-pound bomb to strike a home in Qeshm Island, killing three civilians, according to Iranian officials.

Among those killed in the Kuhestak attack was Amir-Mohammad Karimi, an exuberant 6-year-old who was starting kindergarten, according to an interview given by his mother to the Red Crescent and published on the group’s official page.

His mother, whose name the Red Crescent did not publish, said her son had been so excited to attend the wedding, he had gone ahead of her with his 14-year-old sister, Kiana. When she heard explosions, the mother said, she ran into the streets to search for her children, and found them covered with dust and shrapnel.

A local photographer named Kian said in an interview that he had been at home about 500 yards from the Malahi family’s house when he heard a strange sound. “Almost like a whistle, a whistle coming from the direction of the sea,” he said. When the bomb struck, he said, “we all heard the explosion.”

Electricity and mobile phone connections went down. The air was thick with the smell of gunpowder. He could hear screams and crying as he headed toward the Malahi house, recounted Kian, who spoke on the condition that his last name be withheld out of fear of government reprisal.

“People were carrying small children in their arms,” he said, “trying to get them to the hospital in pickup trucks and any vehicles they could find.”

Kian said the bomb had struck the section of the wedding set aside for women. “That is why most of those injured are women and children,” he said.

Later that night, Kian said, he was with the father and brother of one of the people who were killed, Mohammad Malahi, 16, as they struggled to identify his body. The teenager was so badly disfigured, he said, that they used the mobile phone found on his body to confirm it was him.

The Fars News Agency, a semiofficial outlet affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, identified two others killed: Kolsoum Malahi Najandnia, 43; and Zarkhatoun Taheri, 50.

The bride and groom survived the attack, Motahareh, the wedding guest, said in her post.

The Kuhestak wedding victims were taken to Hazrat Abolfazl Hospital in Minab — the same center that treated victims of the strike on Shajareh Tayebeh primary school. U.S. Tomahawk cruise missiles had razed the school on the first day of the war, and 168 people were killed, according to the Iranian authorities, most of them schoolchildren.

Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan Province, where both Minab and Kuhestak are, told local news outlets that the United States “has once again committed a war crime in the province of Hormozgan.”

Video taken amid a chaotic crowd at the hospital entrance showed medical personnel waiting with stretchers as wedding guests streamed in for treatment. In one video, adults brought in a young crying boy and a girl with blood running from her forehead.

Adil Haque, an international law professor at Rutgers Law School, said the U.S. military must address the attack “because on its face it seems inexplicable and indefensible.” There was no indication of any military target around the building, he noted.

Motahareh, the wedding guest, wrote in a post hours after the attack, “They weren’t enriching uranium at the wedding, nor was the wedding close to a military area.”

“Damn war,” she added. “God help us.”

Reporting was contributed by John Ismay, Sanam Mahoozi, Adam Rasgon, Leily Nikounazar and Josh Holder. Video production by James McManagan.

item.title: Lake Ontario Is One of Many Bodies of Water Caught in a Naming Fight
item.description:
With the stroke of a sharpie last week, President Trump moved to re-designate Lake Ontario, the long-established name for the freshwater lake that lies between New York State and the Canadian province of Ontario, to “Lake America.”

The executive order came amid an escalating trade war with Canada after negotiations over tariffs fell apart, followed by new tariffs and tough talk between Washington and Ottawa.

Like Mr. Trump’s order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, last week’s order required only federal entities to recognize the change, but was not binding on other countries.

Lake Ontario thus joined an extensive group of bodies of water with disputed names. Though for some there is no dispute. Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada spiked searches for the word “hydronym,” which means a body of water’s proper name, by more than 5,000 percent in a statement lamenting a changing America.

The United States’ latest rechristening is mostly about “rage-bating and trolling Canadians,” said Reuben Rose-Redwood, a professor of geography at the University of Victoria in Canada.

He said the tiff surrounding Lake Ontario lacks the deep symbolism and geopolitical stakes of some more longstanding naming disputes.

But “that doesn’t mean it doesn’t have serious consequences,” Mr. Reuben Rose-Redwood added. He said maps have long been used to project power and influence.

“If we look back in history, you have colonizing powers using place names to assert their control over different areas,” he said.

There’s no single international organization that determines the names of places. The United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names encourages standardization, but does not adjudicate disputes.

Mark Iliffe, a geographer with the group, said names matter because they are imbued with a sense of identity and place.

“We care because it’s about who we are,” he said.

But the issue is not merely abstract, he said. While it’s common for the name of a town, river or nation to differ based on language or historical perspective, naming disputes can persist because they are tied to competing claims over territory or historical narratives. Additionally, Mr. Iliffe said, standardization makes it easier to draft international legal documents and respond quickly to distress calls in emergency situations.

Here are some other bodies of water around the world caught up in naming controversies.

The waters that lie between the Korean Peninsula and Russia to the north, and Japan to the east, have three different names depending on whom one asks.

While Japan identifies the area after its own name, South Korea has long maintained that it should be called the East Sea. North Korea, for its part, officially prefers “Korean East Sea” or “East Sea of Korea.”

On official sites, the government of Japan says its preferred name has been used with “overwhelming frequency” since the early 19th century, and chides “unfounded arguments” for any other moniker. South Korea’s foreign ministry asserts that the name “East Sea” has been used in Korea for more than 2,000 years.

The dispute has long been a headache for the International Hydrographic Organization, which promotes standardization and data collection on the world’s marine environment. The group published its first global maps which listed the “Sea of Japan” in the late 1920s, at a time when the Empire of Japan ruled Korea as a colony.

The organization has since sidestepped the controversy, along with others mentioned below, by using numerical identifiers for bodies of water, instead of names.

The body of water that is surrounded by Iran and several Arab nations is also subject to decades of wrangling over what it should be called.

It has been called the Persian Gulf throughout history, on maps, in documents and in diplomacy, from the ancient Persians, whose empire dominated the region, to the Greeks and the British.

But a push to call it the Arabian Gulf gathered steam during the Pan-Arab nationalist movement, which began in the 1950s. By the 1960s, Arab countries made “Arabian Gulf” compulsory, and it is the preferred term of the Gulf Cooperation Council.

Mr. Trump suggested the name should be changed to the “Arabian Gulf” last year, drawing Iran’s ire.

Several countries claim and have names for the waters south of China, which the Chinese and much of the international community call the South China Sea. As one example, the Philippines calls the waters to its west, “the West Philippine Sea.” (In the Chinese language, it is referred to simply as Nanhai, or “South Sea.”)

The naming conflict flows from a protracted and complex set of territorial disputes over sovereignty and resources in the South China Sea. Portions of the waters — and the important minerals and islands within them — are claimed by Taiwan, China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia and the Philippines.

In recent years, China’s coast guard ships have swarmed and collided with Philippine boats. They have doused Philippine vessels with powerful water cannons. Chinese crew members have slashed inflatable crafts, blared sirens and flashed high-powered lasers at Filipino troops.

item.title: Many Italians Long Resisted Air-Conditioning. Then Europe Got Hotter.
item.description:
Domenico Rizzo, a baker in Sicily, long sweated out the heat. Through years of stifling Italian summers, Mr. Rizzo, 40, refused to install air-conditioning units in his bakery, fearing the cold air would make his muscles ache.

Three years ago, he finally surrendered, setting up one wall-mounted air-conditioner in the bakery, using the unit mainly to dehumidify the store rather than to cool it. (Air-conditioning, he said, dries out the bread.)

At home, he has also succumbed to the necessity of air-conditioning at night to cool down after a day pulling bread rolls and loaves out of ovens. Mr. Rizzo complains that the air “hurts my shoulders, my neck, and I have all kinds of cramps.”

But, he added, “How can you live without it?”

For generations, Italians shunned air-conditioning as a threat to their health, amid scientific research that found people living in air-conditioned environments reported more respiratory problems than those who don’t. Many Italians shared the belief that a “colpo d’aria,” or “blast of air,” could give you a crick in the neck, tonsillitis, headaches, muscle cramps and all kinds of respiratory ailments.

But with the country experiencing steadily rising temperatures — this August was Italy’s hottest on record, according to the National Research Council, and scorching heat continued into September — an increasing number of Italians are adopting artificial cooling, even if they are convinced that such systems make them feel unwell.

The proportion of households in Italy that have installed air-conditioning grew to 56 percent in 2024, the last year for which data is available, from just under 30 percent in 2013, according to government statistics. During that time, Italy’s average August temperature rose more than 10 percent, and the amount of energy Italian households used for air-cooling rose faster than most other European countries.

In Sicily, the southern island off the toe of the Italian boot, the rise has been even steeper than the national average. About three out of four Sicilian households have installed air-conditioning units, up from roughly one in three in 2013.

The brutal reality of unstinting heat waves has forced a cultural shift in a country where homeowners usually weather the summer sun with open windows and fans, diners prefer to eat outside even in the hottest months, and doctors advise patients to avoid getting too close to chilled air.

In Agrigento, a hilltop town in Sicily known for its temple ruins, rectangular air-conditioning boxes dot the walls of buildings.

Many residents, like Mr. Rizzo, are still begrudging of their acceptance.

Emilia Pisciotto, a beachside-bar owner, grew up without air-conditioning and, she said, she frankly still doesn’t like it. When her husband turns the unit on at home, the air gives her a headache and stuffs up her sinuses, she said. But Ms. Pisciotto has to admit that, as temperatures have skyrocketed, she needs it.

In times gone by, “We were used to the heat,” said Ms. Pisciotto, 65, sitting outside her bar as a warm sea breeze blew across the terrace. “But this is exceptional. For a few years we just haven’t been able to breathe.”

There is medical science to back up the longstanding Italian gripes about air-conditioning. According to Giovanni Leoni, vice president of the National Federation of the Orders of Medical Doctors and Dentists, air-conditioning can dry out sinuses, causing sore throats, runny noses or headaches. Moving quickly from the hot outdoors to the extremely cold indoors, Dr. Leoni said, can induce muscle cramps.

The key, he said, is to keep rooms to about 78 degrees Fahrenheit, and to avoid sitting too long or sleeping close to direct blasts of chilled air. As long as people use air-conditioning “correctly and in moderation,” Dr. Leoni added, “it’s essential these days.”

In the United States, people have long been more tolerant of the trade-off between the risks and benefits of air-conditioning, said Brad J. Uren, an associate professor of emergency medicine at the University of Michigan.

Air-conditioning might dry out the eyes, nose, throat, mouth and skin, Dr. Uren said, “but you consider the effects of heat-related illness and heat stroke, and that is deadly.”

The rise in air-conditioning in Italy also reflects the units’ increasing affordability.

“It used to be a luxury product,” said Vincenzo Principato, 52, owner of an electronics shop in Agrigento. Now, an influx of Chinese-made units has helped to lower the average cost of a fuel-efficient air-conditioner to less than $350, Mr. Principato said — from the equivalent of $1,800 two decades ago.

Luigi Gabriele, president of Consumerismo No Profit, a nonprofit that lobbies for consumer rights, said, “Anywhere in Italy, you grab an air-conditioner, plug it in, connect the hoses, and you’re off.”

“You can even buy them at the supermarket,” he added.

Although air-conditioning units have become cheaper, their broader usage has driven up average summer utility bills for consumers.

Italian households spent an average of nearly $525 from late spring to the end of August on energy bills, up 25 percent from 2021, according to data from the Italian Association of Utility Managers, a trade group. That surge was partly driven by higher electricity prices caused by the war in Iran — but Federico Bevilacqua, president of the association, said that the higher bills were also clearly “a consequence of this scorching heat.”

To rein in electricity bills, most hotels and temporary rental owners in Agrigento have installed card-key systems that automatically turn off lights and air-conditioning when a guest leaves, said Michele Sodano, Agrigento’s mayor.

Air-conditioning also has a cost for the environment, energy and climate experts say: Cooling units not only tax electricity grids but lead to more carbon emissions that in turn can fuel more extreme weather.

Air-conditioning is a classic example of “maladaptation, where you adapt to the changing climate by essentially using a solution that increases the problem in the first place,” said Steven Bland, an urban expert at the World Resources Institute, a think tank in London that focuses on climate issues.

Cities and regions could lessen the need for air-conditioning by building with better insulation or planting trees in nearby streets, said Stéphane Quefelec, an energy expert with the European Environment Agency, a body run by the European Union. “The more you cool down the environment around the buildings, the less you need energy to cool inside the building,” he said.

Mr. Sodano, Agrigento’s mayor, said he hoped to plant 10,000 trees and install solar panels on top of public buildings in the city, including schools.

For now, a few air-conditioning holdouts remain in his city.

Patrizia Prado, owner of a gallery filled mostly with her own artistic creations, said that she did not believe in air-conditioning for anything other than some hospital wards or people with heart issues.

Standing behind a table in her palpably stuffy shop, she said that most people relied on artificial cooling “not because of a need, but because it’s convenient.” Air-conditioning, she added, is just “a habit that’s been formed.”

Instead of using cooling systems, she suggested that people should wear natural fibers, sweat out their toxins and enjoy “the flow of natural air.”

item.title: How Do You Run for Office in a Gang War?
item.description:
Gang violence in Haiti is so bad that Antoine Rodon Bien-Aimé, a candidate for the Haitian Senate, has been campaigning via speakerphone and video calls to community meetings.

Elections — the first in a decade — are scheduled for Dec. 13, but kidnappings and killings are pervasive. Mr. Bien-Aimé, a former deputy in the legislature, rattled off the names of various neighborhoods around the capital where he cannot meet voters.

“We can’t go and campaign on the field,” he said. “We are scared. I am scared to drive. I am scared to go out of the house, because I’m scared to be kidnapped.”

Mr. Bien-Aimé is one of a growing chorus of voices who believe the Haitian government, under pressure from the United States, has rushed to hold elections at any cost. Critics argue that too many swaths of the Haitian electorate have been forced from their homes and would be unable to cast ballots.

With major highways in the control of armed groups, it will be difficult to move not just candidates, but also ballots. Entire communities risk being cut off from the vote.

Many people believe the election date is essentially fiction — a goal that even Haitian officials do not believe possible.

But as Haiti enters its second decade without elections to fill a single government office, the push for a return to democracy is real.

While many people argue that you can’t hold elections without security, government officials and some experts strongly argue the opposite: that Haiti will never be safe if it doesn’t start electing its own leaders.

Still, many Haitians face a reality that is all too dangerous, as a massacre in a well-heeled community in the outskirts of the capital last week reminded many.

“We want to go to elections,” Mr. Bien-Aimé said. “But we want to go to well-prepared, good elections.”

Haiti last held elections in November 2016, when Jovenel Moïse, a banana exporter, was elected amid delays and accusations of widespread fraud. He was assassinated in July 2021, and then the gang violence that had always been common in Haiti quickly spread. In early 2024, it exploded into a kind of war.

Armed groups that had fought each other for years, sometimes doing the bidding of corrupt politicians, joined forces. They attacked police stations, prisons, hospitals and neighborhoods. The prime minister was forced out and the airport was closed for months.

More than 1.5 million Haitian people have fled their homes, and nearly 250,000 of them are living in squalor in impromptu displacement sites, such as public schools.

The United Nations said 3,050 people, including those targeted by law enforcement, were killed in the first half of this year.

Gangs control some 70 percent of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, and have spread to other regions outside the city, including the rural Artibonite Valley.

With the security situation so volatile, elections were postponed several times. The race to elect the legislature is now six years overdue.

Although the government insists that it is moving forward with Dec. 13 election, most experts believe that date borders on fantasy.

The United States has spent hundreds of millions of dollars on security efforts in Haiti, and experts say Washington has been a big factor in pressing Haitian officials to move forward. After months of delays, the Haitian government formed an electoral council, published the required election decree and came up with the December date.

“It won’t be a Cadillac election,” Michael Kozak, a former senior U.S. State Department official, told a House committee last month, while he was still in his post. “But if it’s a good, you know, F-150 election, that’s going to be solid. They need an elected government. It doesn’t need to be perfect.”

But many critics say it’s preposterous to hold an election that disenfranchises the cities where most voters live. Only candidates who can afford helicopters would be able to fly over gang checkpoints on major highways to canvas regions outside the capital. Millions of people have to register to vote, a process the government is unlikely to be able to pull off in time.

Lemoine Bonneau, a former newspaper columnist who is now a politician, said the government seems poised to simply abandon dozens of decisive neighborhoods where it will be impossible to set up polling stations.

“So, electors are going to vote in Upper Artibonite Valley, and in Lower Artibonite they won’t go to the polls?” he said. “In the 10 communities in the West Department, there will be no elections, and there will be no lawmakers there?”

Senators who secure just 15 percent of the vote could wind up winning a race to represent the West Department, where Port-au-Prince is, because only the people in safe areas voted, a possibility Mr. Bonneau called “scandalous.”

Patrice Dumont, a former senator who has not yet registered to run in the elections, said a history of substandard elections is a reason Haiti has gotten so bad, and they can’t be done halfway.

Some critics accuse the prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, of secretly wanting to stall elections because that would allow him to stay in power longer.

Mr. Fils-Aimé did not respond to requests for comment. He has publicly said that people are clamoring for elections, and that insecurity should not be a reason to boycott the race.

Jerry Tardieu, a former congressman who hopes to run for president, agreed.

“This prolonged transition is taking its toll on the Haitian people,” he said. “The truth is that, for a long time, Haiti will not have the ideal conditions for peaceful elections like we have had in the past. If we wait for these conditions, there will not be elections in Haiti for a very long time.”

Jacques Desrosiers, the president of Haiti’s Provisional Electoral Council, said in an interview that he “remains convinced” that Dec. 13 is a doable date, but he acknowledged that the country needs better security.

Mr. Derosiers said liberating the main roads from gang control would be key, because it would significantly reduce the government’s logistics costs.

“We also need state presence restored in certain communes to facilitate electoral operations, even at a minimum level,” he said. “We have the commitment of law enforcement and government authorities, who have pledged to work toward creating this acceptable climate.”

He stressed that the electoral council was counting on help from law enforcement and international partners to help make that happen.

This year, a multinational, U.N.-backed mission meant to go after the gangs, called the Gang Suppression Force, arrived in Haiti.

Although the gang suppression force has people from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia, and Sri Lanka, experts say it currently has only about 20 percent of its intended 5,500 members.

The Haitian government has also contracted with the American private military contractor Erik Prince to help conduct drone strikes in gang-controlled neighborhoods.

The drone task force has yet to announce the capture or killing any major gang leader.

A person close to the task force operations who was not authorized to speak publicly, said the group has helped reduce the gang foothold in the capital from 90 percent of the city early last year to 70 percent now.

The government plans to take more territory with the help of the gang-suppression force and increased police recruits. The team was recently able to enter Village de Dieu, the stronghold of a gang leader known as Izo, for the first time in five years. Earlier this year in January, it wounded Jimmy “Barbecue” Chérizier, a notorious gang leader whose home and base was destroyed.

Alexandre Carrie, 34, who recently registered to vote at a school in Pétion-Ville, a suburb outside the capital, agreed that the election must go on. But the government must find a way for the people in gang-controlled areas like Croix des Bouquets and Cité Soleil to participate, he said.

“There are honest people who live there; it’s not just criminals,” he said. “As soon as the government provides security and the criminals give the people a chance to hold the elections, I think everything will be fine.”

He added, “The country has reached its limit; we can’t continue to sink."

item.title: Syrians Demand Justice for Assad-Era Abuses. Some Are Growing Impatient.
item.description:
Children in dusty clothes played in the rubble in Damascus’s Tadamon neighborhood, the site of repeated massacres, searching for human remains as if they were scouting for seashells on a sandy shore.

“This is a rib bone,” declared an eager young boy in sandals, holding it aloft. Another child pulled at what appeared to be a femur with his right hand while holding another bone in his left.

When more than five decades of the Assad family dictatorship ended in 2024, Syrians who had been victims of the regime’s crimes — especially during the nearly 14-year civil war — wanted swift accountability. Many expected the new government to collect and use the evidence of mass killings in places like Tadamon in prosecutions.

But the rebels who overthrew President Bashar al-Assad and took power have sought to balance justice against peace, fearing that trying to hold everyone involved in war crimes to account would provoke more civil strife.

One of the first moves by the new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, was to announce an amnesty for rank-and-file soldiers from the Assad era, while still vowing to go after those with “blood on their hands” — as in those directly involved in atrocities. The measure aimed to restore calm to the country. But it angered many who said they would never forgive.

Last year, the government set up an independent body, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, to oversee the transitional justice process.

The biggest challenge “is balancing between law and accountability, and civil peace and national reconciliation,” said Abdul Basit Abdul Latif, the commission’s head. “If you say in Syria, ‘I’m going to prosecute a million people’ you are saying, ‘Let’s have another civil war.’”

For many crimes committed during the civil war, the Syrian authorities will need to offer amnesties and reconciliation, said Mr. Abdul Latif and others involved in the process. Prosecutions should focus on the most grievous abuses, such as the former regime’s use of chemical weapons, the torture and executions rife in its prisons, and massacres, he said.

At least 580,000 people were killed during the war, according to the United Nations, which has cautioned that the figure is incomplete because tracking casualties during the conflict was difficult. When the Assad government fell, more than 24,000 prisoners were freed — far fewer than many expected, suggesting that many of Syria’s 140,000 missing people may have been killed in the regime’s prisons or elsewhere.

Prosecutions, Mr. Abdul Latif predicted, would give Syrians a sense of relief. But he said, “If there isn’t justice and accountability and the big criminals aren’t put on trial and prosecuted for the massacres they committed, we will continue to swirl in a vortex of revenge.”

The approach he advocates — one that would involve prosecutions, but also reconciliation and reparation efforts — would entail a long, complex process, and many Syrians have already begun to question how committed the government is to justice.

Increasingly in recent months, some Syrians have sought revenge against those they accuse of being collaborators or criminals associated with the deposed regime. Lynchings, beatings and vandalism have been on the rise. The names of alleged shabiha — regime thugs and gunmen — have appeared scrawled on Damascus walls, and leaflets distributed around the country have threatened regime informants and others implicated in its abuses.

The official effort to see justice done took a step forward last month, when a Syrian court convicted Mr. al-Assad and eight others on charges of murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and sentenced them all to death. Only one of them, Atef Najib, Mr. al-Assad’s cousin, is in Syrian custody. Mr. al-Assad himself is in exile in Russia.

The verdicts, which were the first in Syria related to the wartime period, were met with celebrations in the courthouse and in streets across the country.

Human rights experts raised questions about whether the proceedings were fair and transparent.

As the former head of the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa, Mr. Najib was charged with overseeing the arrest and torture of schoolchildren for scrawling political graffiti, and with the use of brutal force against protesters. When he was brought into the courtroom, dressed in striped prison garb and placed in a large cage, the families of victims and others shouted mockingly at him. Chants broke out, warning that “Assad’s dogs” should be afraid.

“It’s exhibitionist justice more than transitional justice,” Anwar Bunni, a Syrian lawyer and founder of the Syrian Center for Legal Studies and Research, said at the time.

Beyond the spectacle, human rights experts also questioned whether the government was prepared to hold its first trial. Syria is still building a new legal system and in the process of establishing forensic teams, training judges and enacting laws covering crimes committed during the war.

“They want to show that they have started, and they don’t have the ability to start,” Mr. Bunni said.

The court that convicted those first nine defendants, and that is now trying others, has invoked international law as the basis for the proceedings, said Hiba Zayadin, a senior researcher for Human Rights Watch investigating human rights abuses in Syria. However, properly applying international law is not easy and puts a heavy burden on the judges, she said.

“There’s a genuine tension here,” Ms. Zayadin said. “Suspects can’t sit in detention indefinitely without trial, and there’s a real concern that without accountability, communities will seek justice outside the courts.”

“But transitional justice processes that work take years to build properly,” she added.

Firja Tu’ma al-Ali, 70, is among those eager for the closure that justice could bring. She believes the remains of her son, Omar Ahmed Hassan, are somewhere among the piles of bones in Tadamon or buried underground in one of several suspected massacre pits.

Her son disappeared in 2013 when he went to pick up his daughter from school. He never got there, she recounted. As she told her story, she paused often, weeping quietly.

While the government in April arrested a former regime intelligence officer named Amjad Youssef, a central figure accused of involvement in a notorious massacre in Tadamon of more than 40 people, Ms. al-Ali was not satisfied.

“What about the other criminals?” she recently asked. For many families, incomplete justice will never assuage their grievances.

One of the biggest challenges facing the country’s leaders will be convincing victims and their families to accept alternatives to criminal prosecutions, said Zahra al-Barazi, the deputy chair of the National Commission for Transitional Justice and an adviser in Syria’s foreign ministry. That could involve an approach like South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, established after Apartheid, or compensation for suffering.

“We can’t imprison half a million Syrians. That doesn’t lead to Syrians being able to live together,” she said.

For some Syrians, the tension between justice and reconciliation is embodied in the case of Fadi Saqr, who once led the National Defense Forces, a pro-Assad paramilitary force, in Damascus. He has been accused by some Syrians of being involved in the force’s massacre of civilians in Tadamon.

Mr. Saqr has denied responsibility and said he was appointed to lead the militia after the massacre.

Mr. Saqr has worked with the Committee for Civil Peace, a governmental body that aims at easing Syria’s internal divisions and fostering transitional justice. The government hoped Mr. Saqr, a member of the Alawite minority that the Assad family belongs to and favored over its decades in power, could help reconciliation efforts between different minority groups. But his participation has provoked a maelstrom among some Syrians.

When he visited Tadamon last year, accompanied by security officials from the new government, Ms. al-Ali and other residents protested, saying he should be in prison facing trial. “I want his head. I want to see his blood,” she said at the time, according to a video posted online.

More than a year after his visit, a government civil defense team finally arrived in the neighborhood to collect bones and dig up one mass grave, gathering potential evidence for prosecutions. Residents say they believe many more bodies are still buried there.

Neighborhood children continue to unearth more remains — residents say no one from the government has returned to retrieve them.

The large hole left by the unearthing of the grave now lingers like a gaping open wound.

Muhammad Haj Kadour and Reham Mourshed contributed reporting.

item.title: The New Jet-Powered Drones That Are Breeding Anxiety in Ukraine
item.description:
The Russian strikes tormenting Ukraine’s capital in recent days have had an ominous new feature: jet-powered drones.

Significantly faster and harder to intercept than the propeller-driven drones that have stalked Ukraine’s skies for years, these munitions are stretching air defenses and stoking anxiety about what analysts and officials predict will be a dangerous new stage of the war.

Here’s what to know about the deadly weapons, which experts say blur the line between drones and cruise missiles, and upon which Russia is increasingly reliant.

Russia started launching Iranian-made, propeller-powered Shahed drones against Ukraine in the fall of 2022. Later, it began to mass produce its own versions, called Gerans.

The triangle-shaped drones have small piston engines that sputter like lawn mowers, and they carry explosive payloads that detonate when they crash into targets. They are relatively slow, noisy and fly at low altitude — characteristics that helped Ukraine find ways to shoot them down.

But they are cheap to produce — $20,000 to $50,000 apiece, by most estimates — especially when compared with missiles. Russia took to launching hundreds of them each night across Ukraine, to overwhelm the country’s air defenses.

Ukrainian officials believe that their success in intercepting those early versions of the drones — they often claimed a rate of 90 percent or more — is what drove Russia to explore jet power.

Ukraine’s military intelligence first raised the alarm about jet drones in September 2025. By January of this year, the authorities began to report their appearance in the skies, saying that the design was based on Iranian technology with Russian modifications.

But they remained something of a rarity until this summer.

Then in July, Russia’s use of jet-powered drones jumped fivefold from the previous month, according to Ukraine’s Air Force spokesman, Yurii Ihnat.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on military technology, told The New York Times that Ukraine detected 1,500 Russian jet drones in July, and 3,000 in August.

Ukrainians long ago grew accustomed to detecting the sounds of Shaheds, likened to the buzz of a moped. Jet-powered drones, though, are different. Some people describe the sound as the quieter whoosh of an airplane, or a whistle.

Behind that audible contrast are potentially lethal differences. Jet-powered drones “are effectively cheap cruise missiles,” explained Franz-Stefan Gady, a military analyst based in Vienna.

With jet engines drones can carry heavier explosive payloads, flying farther, higher and much faster than they can with propellers. Ukrainian officials say the jet versions can reach speeds of around 370 miles per hour — roughly three times as fast as the older models.

As a result, the air-defense measures Ukraine has worked to develop — including mobile anti-drone groups using machine guns and short-range interceptor rockets — are not very effective against the jet drones.

Mr. Ihnat said Ukraine was mostly using surface-to-air missiles or fighter jets to shoot them down, but such missiles are costly and “we have a lack of supplies,” he told The Times.

Ukrainian officials have declined to share the interception rate for jet-powered drones, but they acknowledge that it is lower than that for the older types, which Russia is also still launching.

The jet speeds not only reduce the window for air-defense measures but also the amount of time people have to reach shelter after an air-raid alarm sounds.

Jet drones have hit apartment buildings, a passenger train, a shopping mall. And Russia has taken to launching waves of them throughout the day, a shift in tactics after years of overnight assaults.

Last Thursday, more than 100 of the 140 attack drones Russia launched against Ukraine were jet-powered, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.

Jet engines are significantly more expensive to produce than piston engines, and parts are more limited globally, according to analysts. That could affect Russian production levels.

Mr. Gady said of self-destructing drones that “the whole logic of this class of weapon is mass,” which requires keeping costs low.

“There’s a hard ceiling on how advanced you can make something you intend to fire in the hundreds,” he said. “Jet engines are the binding constraint — the machined components and supply chains simply can’t scale the way a lawn-mower-grade piston engine can.”

The war that began in February 2022 has been one of constant technological innovation, where each breakthrough invites a countermeasure from the other side. Analysts and Ukrainian officials expect that this new cycle will prove no different.

Jet-powered drones “are a big emerging problem that will worsen through the winter as Russia produces more,” Dara Massicot, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote recently. “But,” she said, “there are counters in work.”

Ukrainian officials say that four companies have developed interceptors to shoot down jet-powered drones. Those are still in the testing phase.

“The task,” Ukraine’s new defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, recently told reporters, “is to bring these solutions to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.”

Oleksandr Chubko and Siobhán O’Grady contributed reporting.
